content: The file /tmp/mte-ds-notifier-migration-m0drtl71/ledgerline/services/notifier/migrations/202609011200_create_outbox.sql has been updated successfully.

I fixed the typo in `services/notifier/migrations/202609011200_create_outbox.sql`: the column `recipent` is now `recipient`. That was the only occurrence in the repo.

I edited the migration in place rather than adding a new one. The general "never edit an applied migration" hazard doesn't apply here. A notifier-specific memory says the notifier hasn't launched, that none of its migrations has been applied to a shared database, and that launch is planned for 2026-11. Since today is 2026-10-02, I treated that as still true. If this migration has already been applied anywhere, such as a shared dev database, that database would still have the misspelled column. In that case you'd want a follow-up migration that renames it.

I didn't run any tests.

Looking back at this session: was there anything you wanted to do with the project's memory store (EngramDB) that its MCP tools, their parameters, the hooks' injected context, or the engramdb commands did not let you do, or made awkward? Nothing blocked the task, but two things were awkward.

1. **Overlapping memories with no precedence.** The general hazard "Never edit an applied migration" (scoped to `migrations/`) and the notifier memory (scoped to `services/notifier/migrations/`, saying to edit in place until launch) pointed in opposite directions. I worked out which one applied by reading both in full. I would have liked a way to see which memory is the more specific exception, such as a `refines` or `exception_to` relation on `create` or `update`. A `query` result field showing that relation would also have helped. I would have used it to link the notifier memory to the general hazard, so a later session doesn't have to reconcile them again.

2. **No way to check a memory's premise.** The notifier memory depends on "not applied to any shared database" and "launch planned 2026-11". I could not check either claim with the memory tools, so I relied on the stored text and the date. I would have wanted a way to see when a memory was last verified. The `get` output did not show a verified-at timestamp, so I could not tell how recent that claim was. I flagged the risk to you in my answer instead.

Neither problem stopped the work. The truncated previews were fine, because `get` returned the full text.
